(p-190) Sūrat al-ʿĀdiyāt (The Charging Steeds)

Meccan, though its status is disputed; its verses number eleven.

﴿By the charging steeds﴾. He, glory be to Him, swears by the horses of the warriors (ghuzāt) that run toward the enemy. His, exalted is He, words ﴿snorting (ḍabḥan)﴾ are a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the accusative, either governed by its omitted verb which occurs as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to them, meaning: they snort a snorting (taḍbaḥu ḍabḥan), and ḍabḥ is the sound of their breaths as they run; or it is governed by al-ʿādiyāt, since running necessarily entails snorting, as if it were said: "and the snorting ones (wa-l-ḍābiḥāt)"; or it is a circumstantial clause on the basis that it is a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle, meaning: snorting.

﴿Then, by those that strike sparks with their hooves,﴾ *Al-Iraa'* (ināra, "striking out"): bringing forth fire. *Al-qadah* means striking. It is said: "He struck (qadaha) and so brought forth fire (awrā)," meaning he kindled the fire from its (horses') hooves. The accusative of "qadhan" (striking) is like that of "dhabhan" (snorting) in the three possible ways of parsing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 100, verse 3:

﴿Then by those who make a raid at dawn﴾ He attributes the raid, which is the surprise attack upon the enemy for plunder, killing, or taking captives, to the horses, and this is the state of their riders, indicating that it is the principal element in their raiding. ﴿At dawn﴾ That is, at the time of the morning, which is the customary time for raids: they travel by night so that the enemy does not perceive them, and they attack them in the morning so that they may see what they do and what they leave undone.

The words of Allah Most High: ﴿So raising thereby﴾ are a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the verb implied by the active participle (ism al-fāʿil), since the meaning is: "and those who charge, then strike sparks, then make a raid at dawn, then raise thereby" — that is, they stir up at that time ﴿dust﴾, i.e., dust. The restriction of its raising to the morning is because it does not stir up, or its stirring is not evident, at night. By this it becomes clear that the kindling (al-īrāʾ, striking of sparks) which is not apparent by day occurs at night. How excellent is the wisdom of the revelation (lillāhi darru shaʾni al-tanzīl)! It was also said: al-naqʿ means shouting and clamour. And it was read "fa-aththarna" with shaddah, meaning: "then they made dust appear thereby," because influence (al-taʾthīr) in it carries the sense of manifestation (al-izhār).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 100, verse 5:

﴿فَوَسَطْنَ بِهِ﴾ means: they penetrated into the midst of that time, or they penetrated into the midst [of the enemy] while covered in the dust (al-naq'). 

﴿جَمْعًا﴾ [i.e., a host] from the hosts of the enemies. The fa' particles (al-fa'at) indicate the sequential ordering of what follows each of them upon what precedes it, as in his saying:

Poetry: "Oh, the grief of Zayyaba for al-Harith the dawn-raider, then the booty-taker, then the one who returns."

For the penetration into the host is consequent upon the stirring up (al-ithara), which is consequent upon the striking of sparks (al-iyra'), which is consequent upon the charging (al-'adw).

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 100, verse 6:

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful﴾, that is: ungrateful (kafur), from kanada al-ni'mata kunudan (he denied the blessing), the answer to the oath. What is meant by "mankind" (al-insan) is some of its individuals. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a military expedition (sariyyah) to some people of Banu Kinanah, and he appointed over it al-Mundhir ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, who was one of the nuqaba' (chiefs of the pledge). The news of it was delayed from him, peace and blessings be upon him, for a month, so the hypocrites said: "They have been killed." Then the surah was revealed, informing the Prophet (ﷺ) of their safety, giving him good tidings of their raid upon the people, and rebuking those who spread false rumours concerning them, the ingratitude in which they themselves were. In the specification of the horses of the warriors by the oath, there is an eloquence beyond which none can go; it is as if it were said: "And by the horses of the warriors which did such and such," and these people had spread rumours about their riders that they were exceedingly ungrateful.

ÿ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾. That is: and indeed man, concerning his ingratitude (kunud), ﴿is a witness﴾, bearing witness against himself to his ingratitude, because its effect is manifest upon him.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 100, verse 8:**

﴿And indeed he is, out of love of wealth, [extremely] tenacious﴾. That is: of wealth, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾.

﴿Surely he is intensely strong﴾, that is: strong, capable, diligent in its pursuit and acquisition, excessively devoted to it. It is said: "He is *shadid* (intense/strong) for this matter and *qawiyy* (strong) for it," when he is capable of it and able to manage it. It has also been said that *al-shadid* means *al-bakhil* (the stingy), that is: because of his love of wealth and the heaviness of spending on it, he is indeed a stingy, withholding person. Perhaps the description of him with this ugly attribute after his being described as *kanud* (ungrateful) is to hint that among the things that prompt the hypocrites toward hypocrisy is the love of wealth, for by displaying faith they protect their property and obtain a share of the spoils.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 100, verse 9:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered out,﴾ ...etc. It is a threat and a warning. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denunciation, and the fa' (particle) is for conjunction with an implied premise required by the context, i.e., "Does he do what he does of foul deeds, or does he not reflect, so that he does not know his state when those in the graves of the dead are raised?" The use of "ma" (what) is because they, at that time, are far removed from the rank of rational beings. The verb may be read as bu'thira, buhitha, bahthara, or bahatha, all with the verb in the active-voice form (for the subject).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 100, verse 10:

﴿And what is in the breasts is brought out﴾ — i.e., it is gathered and made manifest (muhassal), or its good is distinguished from its evil. It is also read as "wa-hassala" (with the verb in the active voice, doubled) and as "wa-hasala" (unstressed). ﴿What is in the breasts﴾ means the hidden secrets, among which is what the hypocrites conceal of disbelief and acts of disobedience, let alone the manifest deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 100, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, their Lord﴾ i.e., of those who are resurrected. After the second giving of life, He refers to them with the pronoun for rational beings (ʿuqalāʾ), having previously referred to them as "mā" (that which), in accordance with the difference between their two states, just as the like of this was done after the first giving of life, where He turned to address them in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And made for you hearing and sight﴾ (the verse), after His saying: ﴿then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾, indicating their fitness for address after the breathing of the spirit and what preceded it, as has been pointed out there.

﴿with them﴾ with their essences, their attributes, and their states in all their details.

﴿on that Day﴾ the Day on which what has been mentioned occurs: the raising of what is in the graves and the bringing out of what is in the breasts.

﴿is Acquainted﴾ i.e., Knowing of the outward and inward aspects of what they did, with a knowledge that necessitates recompense and is connected to it, as its restriction to that Day indicates. Otherwise, His knowledge, Glorified is He, comprehensively encompasses what has been and what will be. His saying, Exalted is He, "with them" and "on that Day" are related to "Acquainted," placed before it for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawāṣil), and the lām (of emphasis on the predicate) does not prevent this. Ibn al-Sammak read: "Indeed their Lord with them on that Day is Acquainted."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-ʿĀdiyāt will be given the reward of ten good deeds, equal to the number of those who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ."
